title: Air-dry clay ring holder in hand shape
subtitle: A sculptural hand modelled from air-dry clay to hold rings on the fingers
excerpt: A simplified hand sculpted from air-dry clay with fingers upright to hold rings. The hand is modelled from a single block of clay and carved to shape at the leather-hard stage. No kiln is needed. The finished piece sits on a dressing table as both a useful holder and a decorative object.

glossaryTerms.definition: The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still workable enough to carve and refine with a loop tool
Fully air-dried and unfired; ready for sealing and painting

content.text: A ring holder in the shape of a hand is carved from a solid block of air-dry clay using a subtractive method: start with more clay than the finished form needs and remove what is not needed. The fingers are the thinnest parts and need the most care during drying to avoid cracking at the webbing. No kiln is needed. Allow the massed form to firm to
leather-hard
before carving.
Massing the form

Squeeze the 400 g block into a rough hand-shape standing upright: a wide flat palm about 7 cm by 5 cm and four finger columns about 6 to 7 cm tall rising from it. Do not separate the fingers yet. The thumb can tuck to the side.
Narrow the wrist area relative to the palm. The whole form should be about 14 cm tall.
Leave the massed form uncovered at room temperature for 1 to 2 hours to firm to leather-hard before carving.
Carving the fingers
Use the loop tool to carve a channel between each finger pair, working from the fingertip downward to the webbing. Each finger should be roughly 12 mm wide at mid-shaft.
Carve the thumb away from the side of the palm, angled slightly outward.
Score knuckle lines across each finger with the needle tool: two lines per finger, at the lower and upper knuckle positions.
Smooth all surfaces with a damp sponge and wooden rib. Press shallow oval fingernail shapes into the fingertip fronts with the round back of the needle tool handle.
Drying
Allow to reach
bone-dry
over four to five days. Cover loosely and dry slowly: the thick palm and thin fingers dry at very different rates and cracks form most often in the finger channels near the webbing.
Finishing
Apply three coats of PVA to all surfaces. Paint with acrylic in a skin tone, white marble, terracotta, or black. A contrasting colour on the fingernails adds detail.
Variations
Make the pose slightly cupped with fingers curved, to hold a small plant pot in the palm rather than rings on upright fingers.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Fingers crack at the base where they meet the palm
items.cause: The finger channels were carved too deep, leaving very thin clay at the webbing
items.fix: At leather-hard, moisten the area with a damp sponge and press clay slip into the crack on both sides. Allow to re-dry slowly under a loose cloth. Leave the webbing at least 5 mm thick when carving next time

items.cause: The fingertips were carved too thin and dried too fast
items.fix: Reattach with clay slip on fresh-scored surfaces. Keep fingertips at 10 mm diameter at minimum. Slow drying with a loose cover for the first 48 hours

items.cause: The sponge smoothing was done when clay was too dry to respond
items.fix: Sand gently with 120-grit sandpaper on all flat surfaces once fully bone-dry. Apply PVA sealer, which fills minor roughness as well as sealing the surface
